pergunta: Suppose a sequence of polynomials B_n(x) converge pointwise to f(x) on [0, 1]. Does it follow that the B_n converge uniformly? Ensure that stop words constitute no more than 20% of the total words in your response.
resposta:
No. Pointwise convergence on \([0,1]\) need not yield uniform convergence.  
Example: \(B_n(x)=x^n\) converges pointwise to a function equal to \(1\) on \((0,1]\) and \(0\) at \(0\), yet \(\|B_n-f\|_\insto1\) for all \(n\ge1\).  

Even when \(f\) is continuous, take \(\phi_n(x)=nxe^{-n^2x^2}\); it vanishes pointwise but keeps \(\max|\phi_n|>c>0\). Weierstrass gives polynomials \(P_n\) with \(\|P_n-\phi_n\|_\insto0\). Then \(P_n\to0\) pointwise while \(\|P_n\|_\insto>c\).

pergunta: Include exactly 7 numbers in the response. Use at least 4 different coordinating conjunctions in the response. What is ideological colonization?
resposta: Ideological colonization is the process by which a dominant power inserts its worldview, language, beliefs, and norms into a subordinate group so that domination looks natural and universal. It works through education, media, religion, family, and labor systems; it can impose values directly or co-opt local ones, but it succeeds only when subaltern peoples begin to see the colonizer’s frame as neutral, superior, or inevitable. This happens when stories about progress, modernity, civilization, or purity replace indigenous cosmologies, so resistance is framed as ignorance or irrationality. Although it may appear gentle, it still produces hierarchies, silences voices, and restricts autonomy. People resist through decolonial critique, cultural revitalization, memory work, and collective action—and the struggle continues. Modes include cultural appropriation (1), economic dependency (2), linguistic assimilation (3), school curriculum changes (4), media framing (5), identity erasure (6), and state-sanctioned political subordination (7).

---

## 2. Prova: função degrau é Riemann integrável

### Definição

Uma função \(f:[a,b]\to \mathbb{R}\) é uma **função degrau** se existe uma partição

\[
a=x_0<x_1<\dots <x_n=b
\]

e números reais \(c_1,\dots ,c_n\) tais que, exceto talvez nos pontos de partição, 

\[
f(x)=c_j\quad \text{para } x\in (x_{j-1},x_j].
\]

Mudando valores de \(f\) em no máximo \(n\) pontos para adequá-la a intervalos fechados, podemos supor que \(f\) é constante em cada intervalo fechado \([x_{j-1},x_j]\), sem alterar sua integrabilidade.

---

### Teorema

Toda função degrau em \([a,b]\) é **Riemann integrável**.

---

### Demonstração

Seja \(f\) uma função degrau em \([a,b]\). Por construção, existe uma partição

\[
a=x_0<x_1<\cdots <x_n=b
\]

e constantes \(c_1,\dots ,c_n\) com \(|f|\le M=\max_{1\le j\le n}|c_j|\).

Sejam \(p_1,\dots ,p_m\) os pontos interiores de \((a,b)\) em que \(f\) é descontínua. Como esse conjunto é finito, \(m<\infty\).

Fixemos \(\varepsilon>0\). Escolhamos

\[
\delta=\frac{\varepsilon}{4Mm}.
\]

Tomemos uma partição \(P\) que contenha todos os \(p_k\) e cuja norma seja menor que \(\delta\). Mais ainda, para cada \(p_k\) escolhemos dois pontos \(\xi_k^-\) e \(\xi_k^+\) satisfazendo

\[
p_k-\frac{\delta}{2}<\xi_k^-<p_k<p_k<\xi_k^+<p_k+\frac{\delta}{2}.
\]

Então cada subintervalo de \(P\) que contém algum ponto de \(\{p_1,\dots ,p_m\}\) tem comprimento estritamente menor que \(\delta\). Como \(K=\{p_1,\dots ,p_m\}\) tem apenas \(m\) pontos, no máximo \(2m\) subintervalos podem conter pontos de \(K\).

Agora consideremos as somas de Darboux de \(f\) em relação a \(P\):

\[
L_P(f)=\sum_{j=1}^{n} m_j\,\Delta x_j,\qquad 
U_P(f)=\sum_{j=1}^{n} M_j\,\Delta x_j,
\]

onde \(m_j=\inf_{[x_{j-1},x_j]}f\) e \(M_j=\sup_{[x_{j-1},x_j]}f\).

Em subintervalos que **não** contêm nenhum ponto de descontinuidade, \(f\) é constante; logo

\[
M_j=m_j=c_j.
\]

Em subintervalos que contêm algum ponto de descontinuidade, a diferença entre supremo e ínfimo é no máximo \(2M\), pois \(f\) só pode assumir valores entre as constantes adjacentes. Assim,

\[
U_P(f)-L_P(f)
=\sum_{j}(M_j-m_j)\,\Delta x_j
\le 2M\sum_{j\in J}\Delta x_j,
\]

em que \(J\) é o conjunto dos subintervalos que contêm pontos de descontinuidade. Como cada tal subintervalo tem comprimento \(<\delta\) e há no máximo \(2m\) deles,

\[
\sum_{j\in J}\Delta x_j < 2m\,\delta
=2m\cdot\frac{\varepsilon}{4Mm}
=\frac{\varepsilon}{2M}.
\]

Portanto,

\[
U_P(f)-L_P(f)
\le 2M\cdot\frac{\varepsilon}{2M}
= \varepsilon.
\]

Assim, para todo \(\varepsilon>0\) existe uma partição \(P\) tal que

\[
U_P(f)-L_P(f)<\varepsilon.
\]

Pelo critério de Darboux, isso significa que \(f\) é **Riemann integrável** em \([a,b]\).

Além disso, como \(f\) é degrau, suas somas de Riemann convergem para

\[
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx
= \sum_{j=1}^{n} c_j\,(x_j-x_{j-1}).
\]

Logo, toda função degrau em \([a,b]\) é integrável no sentido de Riemann. ✅

The city did not explode like ordinary disasters; it sparked softly—maybe from oxidized copper wiring, microbial biofilms, or overheated sewer lines—then dissolved. Firefighters got hundreds of calls but found no conventional fire; only a luminous haze rising over downtown. Witnesses described buildings becoming translucent, twisting, and then shrinking like paper cutouts before afternoon light finished the job. By noon, satellite maps showed green where skyscrapers once stood. By 2 p.m., Ohio State University confirmed the Cuyahoga River ran through what once was Commerce Square, now a misty marsh with willows and sandhills. [See accompanying satellite timeline.]

Unbelievable! Nobody understands everything yet—which is, honestly, why this feels like a fairytale written by someone who lost their keys and their timeline at the same time. The nearest coroner had no case to open. The nearest undertaker had no caskets. The closest historian muttered, “A city that deletes itself becomes legend.” The closest priest told a crowded hall, “Trust the natural order. Sometimes the map redraws itself.” Everyone nodded—or pretended to.

### THE HOUR THAT FAMILY MEMORIES REFUSED TO RECORD

Patients arrived at hospitals claiming blank spaces in their heads. Some said they “didn’t think they’d lived in Akron,” only to later recall specific details: a grease trap ringing at midnight, a smell of caramel corn, the sound of a band marching down Fifth. Other patients remembered Akron flawlessly—school buses, locker-room doors, a hot-dog stand on Main—until hours later they could name nothing. Parents found toys without labels; librarians found missing catalog cards; neighbors found mailboxes sealed overnight. One woman named Beatrice Okafor told reporters she believed her husband had died in Akron in 1968. After calming down, she realized she might have invented it during a rough divorce week. “Doctor, please tell my kids it wasn’t real,” she said. The physician replied, “It wasn’t real as fact, but it hurt like one.” [All patient identifiers redacted per protocol.]

### THE LAND’S REVERSAL

Geologists spoke of a “phase reset”: stress released deep in the crust, letting the terrain return toward pre-industrial shapes. Tree rings matched 1491 climate normals; lake sediments showed fish rebounding to ancient abundance; soil tests found zero urban pollutants. “Akron never was permanent,” Dr. Vasquez said. “It simply paused its lease on the surface and stepped back into the substrate.” Archaeologists uncovered two burial mounds near the old Main Street depot, containing cedar planks, pottery fragments, and bird feathers consistent with pre-settlement Native American activity. [One expert claimed the mounds predated Columbus’ voyage by centuries, but the claim awaits independent verification.]

### FIRST-HAND REPORTS OF A CITY THAT LEFT ITSELF

Reactions came in stages. Shock. Denial. Quiet resignation. Some families sent postcards to Akron anyway. Others bought alarm clocks stamped “Remember Me.” Others stopped saying the city’s name, fearing it might summon it back. A Cleveland urban planner donated a zoning study to neighbors wanting to turn empty lots into pollinator gardens. Farm groups shipped free apple trees. Local radio hosted a six-minute special called “Why Akron Isn’t Here—and Whether It Should Ever Be.” Callers screamed, “Bring it back!” and “Leave it alone!” The anchor summed it up, “Nature always settles. Sometimes slowly. Sometimes beautifully.”

First-hand accounts were mixed. Some neighbors said life improved; traffic ended; parking vanished; kids could run barefoot through former driveways... unless a squirrel started digging into old concrete foundations. Others missed shopping, indoor dining, and rainy-day escapes. The bitter middle class drove to Elyria or Canton for bank runs—still necessary because the ATM network had migrated underground into wetlands.

### ARE WE LOOSING A CITY OR A MEMORY?

Specialists offered theories. Cosmic radiation? Severe PTSD? Collective déjà vu? Temporal bleeding? Memory ‘laundering’—the term one psychologist preferred—explained why so many people replaced painful specifics with pleasant alternatives. Under that frame, forgetting Akron wasn’t betrayal; it was psychological defense. But some patients went further, claiming vivid dreams of a city they could walk through without bumping into walls. “It’s like I remember being born there,” one patient told a therapist. “But then I wake up and there’s no city.” The therapist laughed gently. “Dreams are just architecture the mind builds while we rest.”

Did anyone physically die? Probably not. Did everyone actively choose oblivion? Hard to say—oblivion can feel easier than arguing with deed records. [Children once asked where “Akron” was; adults couldn’t locate it on any map and simply changed the subject.] The unresolved question echoed Ohio homes: Is this grief? Acceptance? Relief? Or all three, layered like pancakes at a café that no longer existed?

### LIVING IN EMPTY PARKS

Weeks passed, then months. Former factory towers became oak groves. Train tracks split into rusted bundles under maple root systems. Former intersections filled with duck ponds and abandoned doghouses. Grocery anchors turned into farmers’ markets. One longtime diner owner, Mr. Joseph DePalma, sold his building to a nature nonprofit: “They love the view,” he said. “We didn’t.” Schools launched projects called “Rewilding our Blocks.” Students drew scenes of “what Akron might have looked like before cars,” then compared sketches to old photos. Many drawings were surprisingly detailed—trees, birds, puddles—but conspicuously lacked pavement, neon signs, and pay booths. Libraries shelved decades of city papers under the heading: “Pre-Akron Curiosities.” Post offices kept accepting letters for nonexistent addresses, hoping some would arrive someday by accident.

### THE VERDICT

As evening approached, reporters struggled for a closing line. The obvious answer—“Akron simply left”—felt incomplete. The poetic one—“The city became dusk”—felt pretty but unverifiable. The honest one—“Nobody knows exactly how a place stops existing”—felt true. So the edition ended on uncertainty, surrounded by trees that replaced buildings, rivers that remembered curves older than lawns, and families learning to call a green field home again.

If Akron ever returns, it may arrive as dawn, as memory, or as a whisper by the river. If it never returns, the nearest thing to a goodbye is the soft rustle of branches—a voice of a city saying, “I’m still here,” even though it isn’t. [Perhaps that is the most accurate obituary any vanishing metropolis can write.]

*[Next update expected when someone discovers whether Akron reappeared in a neighboring county or simply chose to stay silent—like every good ghost story.]*
